A round white ghost with dark eyes and an open mouth

objects.text: The spirit of someone who has died, said to stay near the places they knew. Almost every culture in the world has ghost stories.

From: everywhere, in stories thousands of years old
Look for: cold spots, footsteps, a figure in white
They want: to finish something left undone
True or not: no proof, but the stories are real

objects.alt: A pale woman with long grey hair, crying out

objects.text: In Irish folklore, a woman of the fairy world whose wailing at night warns a family that one of them will soon die.

From: Ireland (Irish bean sí, 'woman of the fairy mound')
Listen for: a keening cry outside the house at night
She is: a warning, never the cause
Real: keening was a real Irish song of mourning

objects.alt: A hooded figure with glowing eyes, a scythe and an hourglass

objects.text: Death itself, pictured as a hooded skeleton with a scythe who gathers souls the way a farmer harvests wheat.

From: European art, common from the 1300s
Carries: a scythe, and often an hourglass
Why a scythe: death 'harvests' people like grain
In stories: clever heroes try to beat him at games

objects.alt: A floating ball of green light (animated)

objects.text: A ghostly light that floats over marshes at night and leads travellers off the path. Every folk tale agrees: never follow it.

Also called: ignis fatuus, Latin for 'foolish fire'
Look for: a flickering light over boggy ground
Science says: maybe gas from rotting plants, burning
See it in: The Lantern Road and The Haunted House

objects.alt: A sly man in a black hat holding up a glowing carved turnip

objects.text: Jack tricked the Devil, so when he died he could enter neither heaven nor hell. He wanders still, lighting his way with a coal in a turnip.

From: an old Irish folk tale
First lanterns: carved turnips and potatoes
Pumpkins: Irish families found them in America
His name: gave us the word jack-o'-lantern

objects.alt: A pale man in a high red-collared cape with red eyes and fangs

objects.text: A corpse that rises at night to drink the blood of the living. The tales come from Eastern Europe; Count Dracula is from an 1897 novel.

From: Slavic and Balkan folklore
Weak against: garlic, a wooden stake, running water
Sunlight: only deadly since a film of 1922
Real: vampire bats exist, and they are tiny

objects.alt: A green-skinned zombie in a torn grey shirt, arms out

objects.text: A dead body that walks again, without a mind of its own. The word comes from Haitian folklore; the hungry film zombie came much later.

From: Haiti (zonbi), from older West African beliefs
Film zombie: from Night of the Living Dead, 1968
Moves: slowly... unless it is a newer film
Real: a fungus turns some ants into 'zombie ants'

objects.alt: A figure wrapped in linen bandages with glowing eyes and a gold scarab

objects.text: A body preserved after death. Ancient Egyptians dried the body with salt and wrapped it in linen, so the soul would always have a home.

From: Ancient Egypt, over 4,000 years ago
Made with: natron salt, oils, and lots of linen
The curse: newspapers spread it after 1922
Real: the organs were kept in four special jars

objects.alt: A smiling skeleton waving, with a marigold flower

objects.text: The bones inside every one of us. At Halloween and on Mexico's Day of the Dead, skeletons remind us of the dead, often with a smile.

Bones: an adult has 206; a baby has about 300
Strongest: the thigh bone, called the femur
Day of the Dead: Mexico, 1 and 2 November
Real: your skeleton is alive and always renewing

objects.alt: A green-faced witch with orange hair, a crooked hat and a broom

objects.text: In old stories, a person who uses magic, often with a cat, a cauldron and a broom. In real history, innocent people were accused of it.

From: folklore all over the world
Tools: cauldron, broomstick, book of spells
Companion: a 'familiar', often a black cat
History: thousands were unfairly tried, 1450–1750

objects.alt: A shaggy brown wolf-man with yellow eyes and fangs

objects.text: A person who turns into a wolf, usually at the full moon. The idea is ancient: a Greek myth tells of a king turned into a wolf.

From: ancient Greece (King Lycaon) and across Europe
The word: 'were' is Old English for 'man'
Weak against: silver, in later stories
Science word: lycanthropy, 'wolf-person'

objects.alt: A small green goblin with big ears and a stolen gold coin

objects.text: A small, mischievous creature of European folklore that lives in caves and old houses, stealing food and playing tricks.

From: medieval European folklore
Likes: shiny things, tricks, other people's dinner
Cousins: hobgoblins, kobolds, brownies
The word: maybe from Greek kobalos, 'rogue'

objects.alt: A fox spirit with nine white-tipped tails fanned out behind her

objects.text: A fox spirit from Japanese folklore. It grows a new tail every hundred years, and can take human form to help or to trick people.

From: Japan; China and Korea have fox spirits too
Tails: up to nine; more tails, more wisdom and power
Serves: Inari, the Shinto spirit of rice
In stories: its shadow gives it away

objects.alt: A black cat with yellow eyes and a collar with a bell

objects.text: A real cat, of course. In parts of Europe and America a black cat crossing your path is bad luck; in Britain and Japan it can be good luck.

Real: yes, many breeds can be black
Unlucky: an old idea linked to witch stories
Lucky: in Scotland, a black cat at your door
Sailors: kept black cats on board for luck

objects.alt: A brown bat with purple wings spread

objects.text: The only mammal that can truly fly. Most bats eat insects or fruit; only three kinds out of more than 1,400 drink blood.

Real: yes, about a fifth of all mammal species
Finds its way by: sound echoes (echolocation)
Vampire bats: three kinds, in the Americas
Helpers: bats eat pests and spread seeds

objects.alt: A black spider with red markings hanging from a thread

objects.text: Not an insect: spiders have eight legs and are arachnids. Almost all are harmless to people, and they eat a lot of pests.

Real: yes, about 50,000 known species
Legs: eight, and most have eight eyes
Silk: stronger than steel of the same weight
Fear of spiders: arachnophobia

objects.alt: A brown owl with big orange eyes on a branch

objects.text: A night hunter that flies almost silently. In ancient Greece the owl meant wisdom; in other places it was a sign of bad news.

Real: yes, about 250 species
Head: turns about 270 degrees
Silent flight: soft, fringed feathers
In myth: the owl of Athena, goddess of wisdom
